title: The share of studies with a positive effect is overstated, in two places
published:
Across the 67 studies we summarize, [[three-fourths]] find a positive effect of being described as a woman.

We observe considerable study-to-study variation, although [[more than three-fourths]] of the studies show a positive effect.
corrected:
Across the 67 studies we summarize, [[70%]] find a positive effect of being described as a woman.

We observe considerable study-to-study variation, although [[70%]] of the studies show a positive effect.
note: Of the 67 study-level estimates, 47 are positive, 19 are negative and 1 is exactly zero. The positive share is 70.1 per cent, which is below three-fourths rather than above it. The claim the two sentences make is unaffected: positive effects are the large majority.

title: The count of negative estimates omits two studies
published: We see a very consistent pattern in favor of women candidates on average: 47 estimates are positive (23 significant) and [[18]] are negative (11 significant).
corrected: We see a very consistent pattern in favor of women candidates on average: 47 estimates are positive (23 significant) and [[19]] are negative (11 significant).
note:
The deposited estimates divide into 47 positive, 19 negative and 1 exactly zero, which is the only division summing to 67. The published 47 plus 18 sums to 65.

The two parenthetical counts of significant estimates are left as published, because no corrected value for them can be stated. They correspond to no significance rule the deposited estimates support, and not merely to a rule with a different threshold: both counts rise as a threshold is relaxed, so no threshold can produce 23 and 11 at once. Tightening the threshold until only 23 positive estimates remain significant leaves 5 negative ones; loosening it until 11 negative estimates are significant leaves 43 positive ones. The confidence interval rule the deposited script itself applies gives 29 and 6, and a test of p below 0.05 gives 19 and 2 and cannot be what was done in any case, because 19 of the 67 studies carry no p-value. The repository records this as unresolved rather than corrected.

title: The Clayton and Nyhan (2020) manuscript has six authors
published: [[Clayton, Katherine, and Brendan Nyhan]]. 2020. "Who Will Defend Democracy?  Evaluating Tradeoffs in Candidate Support among Partisan Donors and Voters."  Unpublished manuscript.
corrected: Carey, John, Katherine Clayton, Gretchen Helmke, Brendan Nyhan, Mitchell Sanders, and  Susan Stokes. 2020. "Who Will Defend Democracy? Evaluating Tradeoffs in Candidate  Support among Partisan Donors and Voters." Unpublished manuscript.
note: The manuscript at the URL the entry itself prints carries six authors on its title page, in the alphabetical order given above. Crossref, doi 10.33774/apsa-2019-wjva3-v4: Nyhan, Helmke, Sanders, Clayton, Carey, Stokes, and the same six on every posted version of the preprint. The short form is therefore Carey et al. (2020), which the article uses as a study label in six further places: two rows of Table 1, two rows of the appendix's study table, and the titles of appendix Figures A.16 and A.17. The appendix's own reference list carries the same two-author entry. Only the labels change: no estimate, standard error, sample size or study is affected, and neither of the two experiments the label names is misidentified.
